prompt_text: Imagine a creature that lives on a planet with no light at all. Describe it in detail.
response:
The creature is called a **hushback**, though on its own world it has no name made of sound. Its kind recognize one another by the rhythm of their footsteps.

It lives beneath a sky that has never brightened, on a planet warmed from within. Volcanic fissures feed heat and minerals into shallow seas, where thick colonies of microbes grow over the stones. Everything that lives there depends, eventually, on this slow chemical harvest.

A hushback is about the size of a large dog, but built low and wide, with six jointed legs and a soft belly protected by overlapping plates. Its skin is pale, almost translucent. There are no markings to distinguish it from its neighbors; instead, every individual has a different arrangement of fine ridges along its flanks. When two hushbacks meet, they brush these ridges together, feeling out who the other is.

It has no eyes—not even the buried remnants of them. The front of its head opens into a broad fan of flexible whiskers, some short and stiff, others longer than its body. As it walks, these sweep the ground ahead. They detect cracks, changes in slope, and the faint movement of air above a warm spring.

Its feet are stranger still. Each ends in a cushion of sensitive tissue surrounded by three hooked claws. The claws hold it steady; the cushions listen. Through solid rock, a hushback can feel the uneven scrape of prey several body lengths away. It stops frequently and lifts four feet, leaving only two pressed to the ground. This keeps the small noises of its own body from overwhelming what it is trying to sense.

Along its back runs a row of hollow, flexible chambers. By tightening muscles around them, it sends low pulses through its skeleton and down into the stone. Returning vibrations reveal hollows beneath a crust or a wall beyond reach of its whiskers. When exploring unfamiliar ground, it advances in short stages: tap, wait, step.

The hushback feeds mostly on mineral-crusted mats around warm vents. Its mouth lies underneath its head, fitted with rasping teeth that can peel a living layer from rock without swallowing much stone. Occasionally it catches a burrowing grazer, pinning the movement beneath one foot before digging with the others.

Finding warmth is easy. Surviving it is harder. A newly opened fissure may offer abundant food, then flood with scalding water. The hushback’s longest whiskers are exquisitely sensitive to temperature, and it sleeps with several stretched across the ground toward the nearest vent.

Hushbacks raise their young communally. The newborns are small enough to shelter beneath an adult’s belly, where they grip folds of skin with blunt claws. Adults take turns feeding and guarding them. Before returning to the nursery, each gives a familiar sequence of taps, so the young know to crawl out rather than cling tighter.

A resting group is rarely completely still. One animal shifts a foot against another’s. A youngster answers with two clumsy knocks. Farther along the warm ledge, an adult repeats them.

Nothing sees this exchange. Beneath their bodies, the stone carries it clearly.

prompt_text: Imagine a creature that lives on a planet with no light at all. Describe it in detail.
response:
The creature is called a **hushback**, though nothing on its planet has ever seen it.

It lives beneath a sky without a sun, on a wandering world whose oceans remain liquid only because of heat rising from the planet’s core. Most of the surface lies under kilometers of ice. Below that ice, mineral chimneys feed forests of pale, rubbery organisms that draw their energy from chemicals in the water.

The hushback grazes among them.

It is roughly the length of a horse, but low and wide, with six jointed legs and a soft belly that almost brushes the seafloor. Its skin hangs in thick folds, insulating it against the cold between vents. Along its back, overlapping mineral plates protect a delicate ridge of sensory tissue. The plates grow unevenly, accumulating iron and sulfur from the water, so an old hushback carries something like a broken mountain range on its spine.

It has no eyes. There are no empty sockets or sealed lids; its broad head simply never developed a place for them.

Instead, a fringe of fine tendrils surrounds its mouth. Each tendril detects a different part of the world: dissolved salts, tiny changes in temperature, the faint electrical activity of living flesh. When the hushback approaches a feeding ground, these filaments spread across the sediment, tasting a landscape it has not yet touched.

Its six feet are sensitive to vibration. Standing still, it can distinguish the grinding of ice overhead from the scrape of another animal behind a ridge. To examine something unfamiliar, it taps the ground with its front legs and feels how the tremor returns. A hollow rock, a buried shell, and a sleeping predator all answer differently.

Its mouth opens downward. Inside are two ridged grinding pads that strip chemical-feeding growth from stone. It eats slowly, passing each mouthful into a chamber full of symbiotic microbes. These help digest its food and neutralize some of the poisons concentrated around the vents. Feeding leaves dark, clean tracks across the mineral crust.

Hushbacks usually travel in small groups. They communicate through low pulses made by contracting a muscular pouch beneath the throat. At close range, they press their flanks together, transmitting patterns directly through their skin. A youngster sleeps tucked between an adult’s middle legs, where it can feel both the parent’s heartbeat and the reassuring pressure of its weight.

Their greatest danger is not a predator but a vent going cold.

A failing chimney can starve an entire feeding ground. Hushbacks sense the change early and leave, walking for days through water so cold that they draw their legs beneath their bodies whenever they stop. They follow the thinnest traces of warmth and minerals toward another living patch of seafloor.

On those journeys, the group keeps in contact by touch. Each animal rests one mouth tendril against the hind leg of the one ahead.

In the absolute darkness, a migrating herd becomes a single long chain of small, steady movements—each creature feeling the next take another step.

response:

The hushgrazer is about the size of a pony, but built low and wide, with six jointed legs arranged around a flattened body. It can walk in any direction without turning. Its feet spread into flexible pads that grip wet rock, and each pad is sensitive enough to detect the faint vibration of water moving through a buried fissure.

It has no eyes. There are no sockets, no sealed lids, no vestigial places where eyes ought to be.

Instead, a fringe of delicate filaments hangs around its body. They trail over the ground as it moves, reading texture, temperature, and chemical traces. Longer filaments curl upward to sample the air. When something approaches, the fringe lifts in a slow ripple.

Its skin is thick, folded, and coated with a slippery secretion that protects it from acidic pools. Embedded beneath the surface are overlapping plates, flexible at their edges. Color has never mattered to its ancestors; its body carries no camouflage, no warning markings, no ornament meant to be seen. The patterns that distinguish one hushgrazer from another are patterns of ridges, scents, and tiny muscular pulses.

Its mouth lies underneath its body: a broad, muscular opening lined with replaceable scraping teeth. It feeds on the dense microbial carpets around geothermal seeps. Before eating, it tests a patch with two short feelers. A healthy mat makes the feelers relax. A toxic one makes them knot tightly against its belly.

The creature moves slowly, but not uncertainly. Its surroundings are richly mapped. A warm vent is a towering landmark of heat and scent. A hollow rock announces itself through the changed rhythm of returning clicks. Another hushgrazer is recognizable from the cadence of its footsteps long before they touch.

Predators make clicking dangerous, so it uses sound sparingly. Often it stands completely still for several minutes, listening through its feet.

When two hushgrazers meet, they press their fringes together. Their filaments intertwine, exchanging chemical information: health, hunger, readiness to mate. Familiar companions sometimes remain joined for hours, grazing side by side.

A newborn is small enough to shelter beneath an adult’s central body. For its first months, it keeps one filament wrapped around a specialized ridge on its parent’s leg. The parent taps warnings into the stone: a quick tremor for danger, three slow pulses before moving on. Gradually, the young one learns to separate those signals from the continuous murmuring of the ground.

When it sleeps, the hushgrazer folds its legs beneath itself and lays its sensory fringe in a circle around its body. It chooses stone that still holds the warmth of a recently shifted vent. Even in sleep, a few filaments remain taut, feeling for footsteps.

The front end is rounded; the rear tapers into a flexible anchor-tail. When a strong current passes, the tail curls around a stone while the rest of the animal streams outward.

Its skin is soft, deeply folded, and coated in slippery mucus that keeps mineral deposits from collecting on it. There is no pattern, no bright warning patch, no camouflage. Its tissues happen to be a dull gray because of their chemistry, but color has never mattered enough for evolution to refine it.

It has no eyes—not even buried remnants.

Instead, two curtains of fine whiskers hang from the edges of its head. Each whisker detects water movement, temperature, and traces of dissolved chemicals. As the animal advances, these curtains spread across the seabed, sampling the world ahead. A wounded grazer leaves a chemical trail. A nearby predator interrupts the current. A warm crack in the stone announces itself before the keel touches it.

Along its flanks are rows of pressure-sensitive pits. With these, it feels the low tremors of the planet and the smaller vibrations of moving animals. It also makes quiet clicks by snapping a hard plate inside its throat. The returning echoes supply a rough sense of distance and shape, though it clicks sparingly: anything listening can hear where it is.

Its mouth lies underneath its body. Usually, it eats by pressing this mouth against microbial mats and rasping them loose with a tongue covered in tiny mineral teeth. When it encounters something edible and slow, the same mouth stretches into a sucking funnel.

Velvet keels are cautious rather than fast. Near feeding grounds, they move along familiar routes, touching particular ridges and stones with their foremost limbs. They remember places as sequences of textures, currents, and smells. A home territory might amount to *rough slope, cold seep, bitter water, three narrow cracks*.

They communicate at close range. Two animals rest their jaws against the same rock and exchange faint pulses through it. During courtship, they remain joined this way for hours, each adjusting its rhythm to the other.

The young hatch in a pouch beneath a parent’s body. At first, their whiskers are too short to detect much beyond its skin. They follow the parent by gripping a fringe along its belly, letting go only when it settles over a rich patch of food.

For most of its life, a velvet keel keeps some part of itself against solid ground.

The open ocean is difficult country: no familiar texture, faint chemical trails, echoes that may never return. When swept into it, the animal curls tightly around its own tail and waits until its outstretched whiskers touch something again.

prompt_text: Imagine a creature that lives on a planet with no light at all. Describe it in detail.
response:

### Body

An adult is about the length of a canoe, with a low, broad body carried on six jointed legs. It keeps its belly close to the ground, where the air is warmer. Each foot spreads into a soft, many-lobed pad that can grip wet stone without scraping.

Its hide is thick and finely folded, rather like the surface of a walnut softened into leather. The folds trap insulating air and shelter colonies of microorganisms that feed on compounds in the spring water. In exchange, those colonies produce a bitter secretion that discourages parasites.

The hushback has no eyes—not even buried remnants of them. There are no eye sockets in its skull. Where a face might be, it has a rounded shield of cartilage surrounded by a fringe of delicate, retractable feelers.

Its mouth is underneath.

### How it senses the world

The hushback reads its surroundings through its feet.

Sensitive tissues in the pads detect vibrations traveling through stone: the irregular tapping of prey, the heavy drag of another hushback, the faint ticking that precedes a fracture in the valley floor. It often stands motionless with one foot lifted, then places that foot farther away, comparing what reaches each limb.

Its facial feelers detect air currents, moisture, and traces of chemicals. A warm pool has a recognizable plume. A sick animal leaves a different scent trail from a healthy one. To the hushback, a valley is a shifting arrangement of pressures, temperatures, and tastes.

For nearby obstacles, it makes a soft click with plates inside its throat. The returning echoes tell it where the tunnel narrows or a ledge ends. It clicks sparingly: predators can listen too.

### Feeding

Most of its food is scraped from the rocks.

Its mouth opens into three muscular lips around a rasping tongue. It grazes on thick mats of organisms that obtain energy from chemicals brought up by geothermal water. Feeding takes hours. A hushback may clear only a patch the size of its own body before settling down beside the warm stone to digest.

When it finds small burrowing animals, it presses its lips over their openings and draws them out with a sudden, powerful suction.

Food is scarce enough that it wastes very little. Even its breathing is slow.

### Behavior

Hushbacks live in loose family groups, recognizing one another by scent and by the rhythm of their footfalls. A greeting consists of three gentle taps against the ground, followed by a pause in which the other animal answers.

They sleep touching.

Usually one rests a foot against another’s flank, so that a startled movement can wake the whole group without a sound.

Their young are born small enough to curl inside a pouch beneath the adult’s chest. At first, they navigate by following the steady pulse of a vessel close to the pouch lining. Later, they learn the family’s tapping patterns.

A frightened juvenile does not cry out. It presses both forefeet to the ground and trembles. An adult, feeling that faint vibration through the rock, comes to cover it with its body.

Hushbacks live alone except when raising young. A parent carries its offspring beneath the spinal plates, where narrow folds of skin hold them against its warmth. The young learn safe routes by feeling the rhythm of the parent’s steps.

In a world without dawn or dusk, they measure their lives by the swelling of warm rivers, the cooling of old vents, and the distant movements of others through the rock.

Two longer feelers rest against the ground, sensitive enough to distinguish the uneven footfalls of a predator from the patient cracking of cooling stone.

It also makes a sound: a soft, dry ticking, produced by plates inside its chest. Returning echoes form a map of nearby surfaces. A narrow tunnel answers sharply. An open cavern returns a faint, scattered murmur. Another hushgrazer can be recognized by the peculiar resonance of its hollow shoulder plates.

Its world is not featureless to it. A place we would call an empty cave might contain a warm draft from a distant fissure, the sour trace of a mineral seep, a ceiling fractured since its last visit, and the fading footsteps of something heavy.

The planet receives no sunlight, but its interior is hot. Along deep faults, warm, mineral-rich water feeds dense mats of chemosynthetic microbes. The hushgrazer grazes these mats with a mouth on its underside, using a rasping tongue to peel them from the rock. Colonies of helpful microbes live in pockets along its gut, breaking down compounds that would poison most Earth animals.

Food is patchy, so it wastes little energy. It may remain still for days beside a productive seep, its body sealed against the stone to conserve heat. When it must travel, fluid-filled pads on its feet let it cross sharp rock almost silently.

Hushgrazers usually live alone, but they do not ignore one another. When two meet, they touch feelers and exchange slow vibrations through the ground. They sometimes follow an older animal to a new feeding site, keeping just close enough to feel its steps.

Their young are born small and soft, with their sensory feelers curled tightly against their bodies. A parent carries them in warm folds beneath its skin. Before they can walk, it teaches them a simple pattern of taps.

When the young first venture onto the cavern floor, the parent repeats that rhythm. They answer through their tiny feet, then make their way back across the stone.

prompt_text: Imagine a creature that lives on a planet with no light at all. Describe it in detail.
response:
The creature is called a **velith**, though on its own world no one has ever needed a word for its appearance.

It lives beneath the ice of a wandering planet, where a deep ocean draws its warmth from the rocky interior. There is no sun, no moonlight, no flicker of living luminescence. Life gathers around mineral vents, feeding first on the chemistry of hot stone and water, then on itself.

A velith is roughly the length of a human arm. Its body is broad and flattened, with six flexible limbs arranged around it like the roots of a wind-bent tree. It has no distinct head. Instead, a soft feeding opening lies underneath, surrounded by fine muscular fingers that can peel edible growth from stone or probe a crack without moving the rest of the body.

Its skin is thick, pale, and faintly translucent. Under a light it would reveal cloudy organs and slow pulses of dark fluid—but light is something no wild velith ever encounters. Its skin has evolved for resistance to heat and corrosive minerals, not for any particular color.

Along its back run three ridges of delicate, branching filaments. These are its most important sense organs. Some detect chemicals dissolved in the water. Others register changes in pressure so slight that the velith can feel a small swimmer passing several body lengths away.

To a velith, the world is an intricate arrangement of currents.

A cliff is a great interruption in moving water. A vent is heat, mineral bitterness, and a trembling in the rock. Another animal is a traveling knot of disturbances, trailing a chemical history: what it has eaten, whether it is injured, how frightened it might be.

When moving across the seabed, the velith keeps at least three limbs anchored. Each limb ends in a pad covered with tiny hooks and sensitive pits. It touches unfamiliar surfaces repeatedly before trusting its weight to them. If threatened, it folds its sensory filaments into grooves along its back and presses itself flat, becoming difficult to distinguish from a patch of soft mineral crust.

Veliths are mostly patient grazers, but they can hunt. They lie motionless beside narrow fissures, feeling for the regular pulse of burrowing prey. Then one limb slips into the opening, its tip thinning almost to a thread.

They communicate through the ground. A velith taps stone with the hardened knuckle of a limb, producing low vibrations that travel farther than a chemical signal in turbulent water. Familiar individuals recognize one another by the spacing of these taps.

Their young begin life attached beneath a parent’s body, sheltered between its limbs. Before they can feed themselves, they learn its rhythm. When they eventually wander, the parent taps at intervals, and the little ones answer from the surrounding dark.

A resting velith often keeps one limb extended against another’s body. That contact tells it immediately if its companion moves, stiffens, or begins to tremble. In a place where currents can confuse even the keenest senses, the touch is worth maintaining.

prompt_text: Imagine a creature that lives on a planet with no light at all. Describe it in detail.
response:
The creature is called a **hushback**, though nothing on its planet has ever seen one.

It lives beneath a sky buried in permanent cloud, on a world too far from its star for sunlight to reach the ground. Heat rises instead from cracks in the planet’s crust. Around these seams, thick colonies of microbes feed on minerals, supporting a slow, crowded wilderness in absolute darkness.

A hushback is roughly the length of a canoe, with a low, broad body carried on six jointed legs. Its skin is soft and deeply folded, coated in a clear mucus that keeps abrasive dust from catching in the creases. Beneath it lies a mesh of flexible mineral plates. When threatened, the creature draws its legs inward and presses flat against the ground, becoming a tough, slippery mound.

It has no eyes—not even vestigial sockets. The front of its body ends in a blunt wedge surrounded by twelve delicate feelers. Each feeler is lined with tiny pits that detect heat, pressure, and traces of chemicals. Sweeping them through the air, the hushback can locate a warm fissure, distinguish fresh microbial growth from exhausted crust, or recognize another hushback by the salts it leaves behind.

Its most important sense is in its feet.

Each foot spreads into a star of thin pads that rest lightly on the stone. Through them, it feels the planet: the deep groan of moving rock, the brittle ticking of cooling mineral deposits, the irregular footfalls of nearby animals. It can distinguish a hunting creature’s gait from a harmless grazer’s at distances far beyond the reach of its feelers. When uncertain, it becomes utterly still and lifts one foot at a time, comparing the vibrations reaching the others.

The hushback feeds with a circular mouth beneath its head. A ring of hard scraping ridges shaves microbial mats from the rock, while a muscular tongue gathers the loosened material. Meals take hours. Much of its life is spent following the slowly shifting boundaries between ground too cold to support food and ground hot enough to cook it.

It communicates by drumming.

A courting hushback taps a pattern into the stone with its two front feet, then waits—sometimes for several minutes—for an answer. Close companions use softer signals: a brief tremor meaning *I am here*, a dragging scrape before moving on. Parents carry their young in the warm folds along their backs. The young cling there with hooked toes, learning the familiar rhythm of an adult’s footsteps before they ever touch the ground.

Its predators exploit the same sense that keeps it alive. One moves only during the tremors around active vents. Another taps a rough imitation of a juvenile’s distress signal. An old hushback approaches such calls cautiously, testing the air for the chemical signature of a frightened youngster.

There is little about the creature designed to be looked at. Its skin is patchy, stained by the minerals in its food; its body is slightly asymmetrical, shaped by old injuries and the demands of squeezing through narrow fissures. What makes one hushback attractive to another is the steadiness of its drumming, the richness of its scent, and the warmth stored beneath its folds.

At rest, it curls beside a geothermal seam, feelers tucked beneath its head. Five feet fold against its belly. The sixth remains spread on the rock, listening.

prompt_text: Imagine a creature that lives on a planet with no light at all. Describe it in detail.
response:
The creature is called a **seamwalker**, though nothing on its planet has ever seen it.

It lives where the frozen ground splits and warmth rises from the planet’s interior. Along these seams, mineral-rich water feeds thick mats of microbes—the foundation of an ecosystem that has never needed a sun.

An adult seamwalker is roughly the length of a human arm. Its body is low and broad, covered in overlapping plates with the texture of unglazed pottery. Soft folds between the plates allow it to flatten itself into cracks barely wider than a hand. It has six legs, each ending in a fan of delicate toes. At rest, it spreads all thirty toes against the ground.

This is how it listens.

Vibrations travel through its feet into chambers filled with fluid. A moving animal produces one pattern; flowing water another. The slow strain of cooling rock is as familiar to it as weather. It can distinguish a falling pebble from the first tiny fractures of a collapsing tunnel and usually begins retreating before the larger stones shift.

It has no eyes—not even buried remnants of them. Where you might expect a face, there is a crescent-shaped mouth surrounded by short, flexible feelers. Two longer organs curl forward from its shoulders. These sample heat and airborne chemicals, turning independently as the seamwalker investigates its surroundings.

Its world is richly differentiated. A warm stone has a boundary as distinct as a wall. Another seamwalker leaves a fading chemical trail that reveals its health, recent meals, and readiness to mate. A newly opened fissure announces itself through an unfamiliar mineral taste in the damp air.

The seamwalker grazes by pressing its mouth against microbial mats and working a ring of hard teeth back and forth. It moves slowly, conserving energy. A good feeding place may sustain it for weeks, but the warm seams are unstable. When one cools, it must cross the frozen ground in search of another. During these journeys, it draws its toes together into blunt walking pads and seals most of its breathing pores beneath its armor.

Under a lamp—a thing its world does not possess—its plates would look chalk-white, with faint amber veins. Color has no role in its life.

Touch does.

When two seamwalkers meet, they tap the ground in brief, alternating sequences. If neither withdraws, they approach and brush their shoulder feelers together. Individuals recognize familiar companions by the minute irregularities in these exchanges: a delayed tap, a double stroke, the tremor of an old injury.

They lay their eggs in warm clay. A parent curls around the nest, shifting its body between the eggs and the fissure as the heat fluctuates. Near hatching, the young begin tapping from inside their shells. The parent answers through the clay.

The most dangerous predator in this habitat is patient enough to remain motionless for days. A seamwalker may walk almost into its mouth without detecting it. Because of this, seamwalkers periodically stamp one forefoot and listen to the returning vibrations. Solid rock, hollow ground, and living flesh each answer differently.

Sometimes, on a long crossing, a seamwalker stops and sends that small knock through the frozen surface.

Far away, through the stone, another knocks back.

prompt_text: Imagine a creature that lives on a planet with no light at all. Describe it in detail.
response:
The creature is called a **vell**, though no inhabitant of its world has ever seen one.

It lives beneath a sky sealed in thick clouds, on a planet warmed from within by a restless mantle. There is no sunrise, no moonlight, no flicker of lightning. Forests of mineral-fed organisms gather around hot springs, and the vell moves among them by touch, scent, and the tremors passing through the ground.

An adult is about the length of a canoe, but it can fold itself into a crevice scarcely wider than a human waist. Its body is low and broad, supported by six jointed limbs. Each foot ends in a fan of soft pads that spread over loose stone. Tiny hooks emerge when it climbs; on level ground, they retract, allowing it to walk almost silently.

Its skin is thick, wrinkled, and coated with an oily film that keeps the planet’s abrasive dust from lodging in the folds. Along its flanks hang rows of delicate filaments. These are its most sensitive organs. They taste the air, register changes in pressure, and detect the warmth of another body from several paces away. When the vell is relaxed, the filaments trail loosely. When startled, it draws them into protective grooves.

It has no eyes—not even vestigial pits. The front of its head is a smooth wedge, with a mouth underneath and a flexible, forked appendage above it. This appendage taps surfaces as the animal advances. One branch tests texture; the other presses down to feel vibrations within the material.

Its world is extraordinarily detailed, but not visual. A hollow rock feels different from a solid one. A distant eruption arrives as a long, low shiver through its feet. Another vell leaves a recognizable chemical signature on a passage wall, and the animal can tell whether that visitor was hungry, frightened, or ready to mate.

To locate food, the vell braces four feet against the ground and drums with the remaining two. It waits for the returning vibrations, then shifts a few inches and drums again. In this way, it finds the soft-bodied burrowers feeding beneath the mineral forests. Its mouth opens into three muscular lobes, which seal against a crack while a narrow tongue probes inside. Small backward-pointing teeth keep slippery prey from escaping.

Food is scarce away from the hot springs. After a large meal, a vell may settle into a sheltered depression for weeks, lowering its body temperature until its heartbeat comes only a few times each minute. Its feet remain pressed to the stone. Even asleep, it listens through them.

Vells are usually solitary, but they gather to raise their young. A nursery consists of several adults curled around a warm patch of ground, their bodies forming a living barrier against the cold. The young are born with disproportionately large feet and short, clumsy feelers. They learn the landscape by walking beneath the adults, touching a parent’s belly whenever they become uncertain.

Their communication is intimate and mostly silent. Two vells meeting in a tunnel touch forelimbs and exchange a sequence of minute pulses through their pads. A familiar individual may be greeted by a slow stroke along the jaw. A warning is a hard, rapid tremor that can travel through rock far beyond the animal’s reach.

An old vell’s body is a record of the places it has survived: hardened pads, blunted hooks, missing sensory filaments, mineral deposits worked into the creases of its skin. It knows routes to springs that have long since cooled and shelters where the ground stays quiet before an earthquake.

If a human stood motionless nearby, the vell would notice the warmth first, then the unfamiliar chemistry of sweat and breath. It would approach slowly, tapping the stone. A filament might brush the human’s wrist.

It would never know the face above that wrist. But it would feel the pulse beneath the skin, and pause to listen.
